title: Training fair use: Lawfulness depends on particular copying
desc: Separates acquisition, retention, training and distribution while disputing whether noninfringing competition constitutes copyright market harm.

kps.k: AI-training fair use turns on the particular use and competitive purpose, not on a blanket exemption for AI.
kps.d: Kadrey and Bartz find the LLM-training uses before them highly transformative and grant developers summary judgment on those uses. Both accept whole-book copying as reasonable for training despite the books’ protected expression. By contrast, the ROSS district court rejects fair use because ROSS used headnotes to develop a competing legal-research tool; converting text into numerical training data did not make that purpose transformative. That court expressly confines its ruling to non-generative AI. These outcomes distinguish uses and records rather than establish a universal rule for training.

qs.q: Therefore, on this record, Meta is entitled to summary judgment on its fair use defense to the claim that copying these plaintiffs’ books for use as LLM training data was infringement.
qs.a: Kadrey v. Meta — summary judgment for Meta on fair use, with the market-dilution dictum · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: 22           The copies used to train specific LLMs were justified as a fair use.
qs.a: Bartz v. Anthropic — order on fair use: training on lawfully acquired books is fair use; pirated-library copying is not · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: The central disagreement concerns whether noninfringing AI competition can count as copyright market harm.
kps.d: Bartz rejects the authors’ forecast of proliferating competing works as a basis for denying fair use, reasoning that copyright does not protect against noninfringing competition. Kadrey takes the contrary position: mass-produced books in the same topics or genres could divert sales and attention even without copying protected expression. It rejects the analogy to teaching people to write because AI changes the scale and cost of production, while qualifying that some indirect harm remains tolerable. In ROSS, the district court treats competition with Westlaw as substitution; on appeal, ROSS argues that competition between research products does not establish substitution for copyrighted headnotes. The supplied appeal account reports arguments, not an appellate resolution.

qs.q: The Act seeks to advance original                                    15     works of authorship, not to protect authors against competition.
qs.a: Bartz v. Anthropic — order on fair use: training on lawfully acquired books is fair use; pirated-library copying is not · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: But less similar outputs, such as books on the same topics or in the same genres, can still compete for sales with the books in the training data.
qs.a: Kadrey v. Meta — summary judgment for Meta on fair use, with the market-dilution dictum · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Potential training-license markets raise a related dispute over circular reasoning.
kps.d: Kadrey rejects lost fees for transformative training as cognizable harm, rather than allowing the asserted need for a license to decide whether one is legally required. Bartz likewise rejects a licensing entitlement for the training use it finds fair, even assuming the authors’ licensing-market account. The ROSS district court instead recognizes legal-AI training data as a potential derivative market alongside legal-research platforms, without requiring Thomson Reuters already to exploit it. ROSS challenges that market definition on appeal as circular. The contrast partly reflects the courts’ different findings about transformative purpose, not simply conflicting evidence about whether licensing markets exist.

qs.q: Therefore, to prevent the fourth factor analysis from becoming circular and favoring the rightsholder in every case, harm from the loss of fees paid to license a work for a transformative purpose is not cognizable.
qs.a: Kadrey v. Meta — summary judgment for Meta on fair use, with the market-dilution dictum · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: Even                                    22     so, such a market for that use is not one the Copyright Act entitles Authors to exploit.
qs.a: Bartz v. Anthropic — order on fair use: training on lawfully acquired books is fair use; pirated-library copying is not · Regulators & courts · 2025

kps.k: Acquisition, retention, training and distribution require distinct analysis; lawful training does not automatically excuse a pirated library.
kps.d: Bartz separates training from Anthropic’s acquisition and permanent retention of more than seven million pirated books, including books it would never train on. It rejects fair use for that general-purpose library because it displaced purchases, but independently approves one-for-one digitization of purchased books where Anthropic destroyed the originals and did not redistribute replacements. Kadrey rejects an automatic loss based on shadow-library acquisition and considers the identified downloads in light of their training purpose. This difference involves both the courts’ treatment of acquisition and different retention records: Bartz expressly declines to rest on a blanket prohibition against pirated training sources. Neither decision makes bad faith decisive, and Kadrey leaves torrenting-related distribution claims unresolved.

qs.q: United States District Court                                   13           Before buying books for its central library, Anthropic downloaded over seven million                                    14     pirated copies of books, paid nothing, and kept these pirated copies in its library even after                                    15     deciding it would not use them to train its AI (at all or ever again).

kps.k: Evidence of substitution, not general predictions about AI, determines the reach of the rulings.
kps.d: Kadrey’s acceptance of market dilution does not establish that Llama caused it. Meta’s expert found no discernible sales effect shortly after Llama 3’s release, while the authors supplied no empirical rebuttal or meaningful causal link to substitution for their particular books. Neither party’s expert identified regurgitation exceeding 50 words from those books under adversarial prompting. The court nonetheless leaves future harm open and labels its expectation of stronger plaintiff cases as broader commentary; its judgment affects only thirteen authors. Bartz addresses inputs, preserves future output-infringement claims and withholds approval of poorly documented additional copies. The developer bears the fair-use defense burden; gaps in the opposing evidence do not create a general presumption that training is lawful.

qs.q: And Meta presented its own expert testimony explaining that Llama 3's release did not have any discernible effect on the plaintiffs’ sales (or those of other books in Llama's training data), at least in the period shortly after the release.
qs.a: Kadrey v. Meta — summary judgment for Meta on fair use, with the market-dilution dictum · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: And, if the outputs were ever to become infringing, Authors                                     6     could bring such a case.

kps.k: The practical stakes extend beyond output filtering to data provenance, copying records and the boundary between law and editorial expression.
kps.d: The decisions make acquisition records, retention purposes, access controls and evidence about relevant markets important to a training defense. Non-reproducing outputs help but do not alone establish fair use, as ROSS illustrates. Its pending appeal also challenges headnote copyrightability: ROSS argues that accuracy leaves little protectable expression and warns against private control over statements of law. The district court instead finds sufficient originality, while treating the headnotes’ modest creativity as a factor favoring ROSS. For developers whose uses fail fair use, Kadrey identifies licensing and public-domain material as alternatives; its expectations of bulk licensing and contractual adaptation remain predictions, with acknowledged costs and delays.

qs.q: We cannot determine the right answer concerning such copies because the record is                                    15     too poorly developed as to them.

vlens.an: The supplied legal-tech-vendor-voice source supports the proposition that training fair use depends on the particular copying, purpose and alleged substitution rather than a categorical rule for AI. Its central reasoning distinguishes competition between finished legal-research products from substitution for the copyrighted headnotes themselves, stresses that ROSS’s outputs did not reproduce those headnotes, and argues that defining an “AI training” licensing market from the challenged use risks circularity. Material variation appears within the source’s own analysis: although it presents ROSS’s market distinction as its strongest argument, it notes that Westlaw likewise did not sell headnotes separately, complicating any simple separation between the copyrighted work and the commercial product. The account also reports advocacy in a pending appeal rather than an appellate holding. Because the curated evidence contains one source in this professional voice, it establishes that source’s position only and does not indicate prevalence among legal-tech vendors.

qs.q: The question as argued, however, felt even more focused: if ROSS copied protected headnote expression to build a direct legal research competitor, is that market substitution enough to defeat fair use even if the outputs did not reproduce the headnotes?
qs.a: Thomson Reuters v. ROSS Intelligence at the Third Circuit — Interlocutory Appeal No. 25-2153, Argued 11 June 2026 (Decision Pending) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

qs.q: ROSS resisted defining the market as “AI training” or “legal research platforms,” warning that doing so would make fair use circular: any innovative use could be converted into a licensing market simply because the copyright owner, after seeing the use, says it would have licensed that use.
qs.a: Thomson Reuters v. ROSS Intelligence at the Third Circuit — Interlocutory Appeal No. 25-2153, Argued 11 June 2026 (Decision Pending) · Legal-tech vendor · 2026

vlens.an:
The selected judicial sources support the proposition that AI-training fair use depends on the particular copying, objective use, competitive purpose and evidentiary record—not on a categorical rule for AI. Bartz most explicitly separates acquisition, retention, training and format conversion, approving specific LLM-training and digitisation uses while denying fair use for a retained pirated general-purpose library. Kadrey likewise confines its result to the reproduction claims and record before it, separately preserving distribution issues and rejecting any broader declaration that Meta’s training is lawful. ROSS reaches the opposite outcome on fair use but reinforces the same method: it treats the development of a competing legal-research product as non-transformative and expressly limits its decision to non-generative AI.

Material internal variation concerns how that use-specific framework applies. Bartz treats permanent retention of pirated books as an independently non-transformative use, whereas Kadrey considers the identified shadow-library downloads in light of their ultimate training purpose and finds no automatic defeat of fair use on its record. The courts also diverge over market harm: Bartz excludes noninfringing competition and lost training-licence fees for a use already found fair; Kadrey recognizes market dilution from mass-produced noninfringing substitutes as legally possible but finds it unproved; ROSS recognizes both competition with Westlaw and a potential market for legal-AI training data. These differences qualify outcomes rather than displace the shared proposition. Because these are curated judicial decisions, they should not be treated as representative of all courts, regulators or professional bodies.

qs.q: 7          These factors presuppose a “use.” So, at the threshold, a court must decide whether a                                     8     “copyrighted [work] has been used in multiple ways,” then evaluate each.
qs.a: Bartz v. Anthropic — order on fair use: training on lawfully acquired books is fair use; pirated-library copying is not · Regulators & courts · 2025

qs.q: And, as should now be clear, this ruling does not stand for the proposition that Meta's use of copyrighted materials to train its language models is lawful.
qs.a: Kadrey v. Meta — summary judgment for Meta on fair use, with the market-dilution dictum · Regulators & courts · 2025

elens.an:
The selected 2025 rulings support the cluster’s principal proposition that AI-training fair use is use-specific and record-specific, not governed by a blanket rule for or against AI. Their common reasoning separates the objective purpose of particular copies and asks whether the challenged use is transformative, commercially substitutive, and supported by evidence of market harm. Bartz most explicitly separates training, format conversion, acquisition and permanent library retention; Kadrey limits its fair-use judgment to the reproduction claims and evidentiary record before it while treating distribution separately; and the ROSS ruling denies fair use because the protected headnotes were used to build a competing legal-research product, while limiting its analysis to non-generative AI.

Material variation concerns how those principles apply. Bartz and Kadrey approve the particular general-purpose LLM-training uses, whereas ROSS finds the competitive research-tool purpose non-transformative. Bartz rejects fair use for Anthropic’s retained pirated general-purpose library, while Kadrey does not treat shadow-library acquisition as automatically dispositive on its different record. The decisions also diverge on market harm: Bartz rejects noninfringing competition and training-licence fees as cognizable harm for the use it finds fair; Kadrey recognizes market dilution by noninfringing outputs as a possible theory but finds it unproved; and ROSS recognizes both substitution in legal-research platforms and a potential legal-AI training-data market. These differences develop rather than undermine the proposition because they turn on distinct uses, records and market definitions. As a curated set, the rulings show doctrinal variation but do not establish how prevalent any view is among courts generally.

qs.q: 7          These factors presuppose a “use.” So, at the threshold, a court must decide whether a                                     8     “copyrighted [work] has been used in multiple ways,” then evaluate each.
